A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that there is an attractive force between transmembrane protein domains in the lipid membrane that is mediated by a pre-transition effect, and that the magnitude of this force is significantly larger than that which could arise from membrane bending.

we show that a transmembrane protein with hydrophobocity that matches that of a disordered phase embedded within an ordered phase of the lipid membrane stabilizes a microscopic interfacial region of coexistence between the two phases.

we show how a protein in a lipid membrane with a hydrophobic thickness that is not matched to the thickness of the membrane can stabilize a pre-transition interface between ordered and dis ordered lipid domains.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pre-transition effect can be a strong, long-range force for the assembly of transmembrane proteins and that it can be mediated by the size and hydrophilicity of the transmembrane region.
the orderphobic effect is a generic, powerful, and ubiquitous force that can mediate assembly and mobility for a large class of transmembrane proteins and protein complexes.
